speechtext: I would like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Has the attention of the minister been drawn to the article which appeared in the newspaper Le Droit on May 21 dealing with the outbreak of a mysterious disease, which it is reported has already claimed the lives of six cows since last Wednesday and has affected a number of other cows? If so, could the minister tell the house whether his department has investigated the matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: THURSO, QUE.  REPORTED OUTBREAK OF RABIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the press clipping from Le Droit was handed to me this morning, but this disease had come to the attention of the department previously and the health of animals branch prepared a memorandum on it for me on May 20, which I think perhaps I should read to the house. It reads as follows:
Following reports that a number of cattle were exhibiting symptoms of rabies in the Thurso area, departmental veterinarians visited the area and conducted an investigation.
Preliminary reports indicate approximately 900 animals-mostly cattle and a few horses-were vaccinated against rabies. Approximately two weeks following vaccination a number of the cattle began to show partial clinical evidence indicative of rabies.
Specimens collected and examined at the department's animal diseases research institute have so far indicated that the causative agent or virus of rabies is not existent in the affected animals so that the clinical evidence being exhibited by the sick animals is a reaction to the vaccination, and not in fact an attack of rabies resulting from
[Mr. Hees.l
infection. Reports to date indicate that the transmission of rabies from the affected cattle is not possible.
The vaccinations were carried on by a veterinarian in private practice and the department is in no way involved, except that close observation is being kept on the sick animals and laboratory studies on the affected animals are being conducted.
Preliminary reports of the investigation indicate that the private practitioner used vaccine intended and labelled for use in dogs rather than the vaccine designated for use in cattle.
I received a further report this morning that approximately 45 deaths and 40 sick animals have been reported.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Before proceeding with the orders of the day, if the house would permit me one word I should like to refer hon. members to two citations relating to oral questions about public policy. There are many borderline questions, and there were some this morning. For the guidance of the house perhaps I might refer to Bourinot's fourth edition, at page 314, where he expresses this view of the practice:
While explanations of the intentions of the government or of a minister may be asked, their opinion on a matter of policy or of law is not a proper subject of inquiry.
It is perhaps a rather fine distinction between intention and opinion, but it is one that can be drawn and is one that should be kept in the minds of hon. members when they ask questions.
I should like to refer to Beauchesne and also to May, sixteenth edition, page 356. Beauchesne's second edition, citation 339, repeated in the fourth and latest edition as citation 178, reads:
Questions addressed to ministers should relate to the public affairs with which they are officially connected, to proceedings pending in parliament, or to any matter of administration for which the minister is responsible. Within these lines an explanation can be sought regarding the intentions of the government, but not an expression of opinion upon matters of policy.
406	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Inquiries of the Ministry
May I refer also to another rule of the house. I was not in the chair yesterday when a reference was made to the Governor General. Although I am sure that the hon. member who made the reference intended no disrespect of the Governor General, perhaps what was said would be susceptible of that interpretation. For the guidance of hon. members of the house may I refer to standing order No. 35:
No member shall speak disrespectfully of Her Majesty, nor of any of the royal family, nor of His Excellency or the person administering the government of Canada: nor use offensive words against either house, or against any member thereof.
May I refer also to a comment on the practice which is found in May's sixteenth edition at page 457:
Unless the discussion is based upon a substantive motion, drawn in proper terms, reflections must not be cast in debate upon the conduct of the sovereign, the heir to the throne, or other members of the royal family, the governor general of a dominion, the Speaker, the chairman of ways and means, members of either house of parliament, or judges of the superior courts-
-and so on.
Since there are many new members in the house, I thought it desirable to refer to the rules and the practice, so that in the future members would be careful in making references of that kind.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last evening at 10 o'clock I was making some comments concerning markets for Newfoundland fish. I am informed that during the year 1956 the total exported by the Newfoundland Association of Fish Exporters Limited, more popularly known as NAFEL, was about 783,173 hundredweight. Of this amount 14 per cent was exported to Europe, 25 per cent to the British Caribbean, 20 per cent to other Caribbean areas, 1 per cent to South America and 40 per cent to the Canadian mainland and to the United States.
I believe every effort should be made not only to retain these markets but to expand them, even if it is necessary to increase the support prices for fish above the levels existing at the moment in order that the fishermen may be able to get a fair return for their labour, and so that at the same time it may be possible for Newfoundland to meet the maximum price which these markets are able to pay. There may even be some wisdom in providing extra support for fishery products of high quality.
May I move on to a few comments regarding the bait service in Newfoundland, and I am going to make this rather brief. The bait service which was initiated in the early thirties was a great help to the Newfoundland fishermen, but over the years since then the structure of the Newfoundland fisheries has changed in a marked degree and the bait service as it exists at the moment is no longer adequate to look after the needs of the fishermen, particularly in certain areas which up
The Address-Mr. Batten to this point have not been served by the bait service. It is not adequate in the sense that without bait being supplied, our fishermen are not able to begin to work earlier in the year or to carry on the industry late in the fall.
I am not going to make extended remarks on the problem, but it is a very serious one for us in Newfoundland. I know the Minister of Fisheries has the problem under study, and I hope it will not be too long before the minister will be able to present to the house a report on his study and a summary of his proposals.
Before leaving my comments on the fishing industry I should like to make one comment regarding unemployment insurance for fishermen. To our fishermen this has been a great boon, for I think it will help to retain good fishermen in the industry who will be able to make a good living and at the same time make a fine contribution to the industry itself. But my problem at the moment is one of unemployment insurance and school attendance.
I do not propose at the moment to enter into a discussion of education, but in passing I should like to say that I have been very pleased to note the number of hon. members who in their speeches in this debate have made some reference to education. I certainly agree that there is a problem that some time in the near future the country is going to have to face, not in the sense of getting into any race with Russia, not in the sense of having our educational system weighted on the science side at the expense of the social sciences and humanities, but in the sense of providing Canadians with better educational opportunities.
However, I am getting away from the problem I want to discuss, a problem which is a much simpler one than that. Over the last few months a problem has arisen involving a number of young men, and to be fair I must say it is not a large number, who owing to the number of stamps they acquired during the last fishing season were able to qualify for unemployment insurance. These men live in an area where normally they are able to obtain winter employment in the logging business. During the last few months this type of employment has not been so regularly available as it had been before. These young men were at home with nothing to do and decided that they would attend the local school for a few weeks to improve themselves as much as they could from attendance at that institution. The moment they attended the local school they were disqualified and not permitted to draw their unemployment insurance, on the assumption that they were not available for work.

The Address-Mr. Batten
I do not think that anybody who attends school on a temporary basis can be considered as out of the labour market, and I would rather feel that young people who decide they are going to use their free time to attend the local school should not be penalized by being disqualified for unemployment insurance. In fact I would go considerably further and say that any young person who has been previously employed in an insurable occupation and who decides to go to high school or even to university should not lose the credit he has built up. I will agree that for the time being a university student, having committed himself for a year, may be temporarily not available for work, but at the same time he is preparing himself for better work in the years that lie ahead.
I bring this problem to the attention of the Minister of Labour, and I hope he will give some attention to it.
May I now move on to one or two other points, and I see I shall have to make my remarks concerning them rather brief. On the west coast of Newfoundland Canadian National Telegraphs have not been able to provide the outlying districts with communication services that are adequate to meet the need. Time was when this section of Newfoundland was well served by a communications system. Over the years part of it has been dropped and up to this point the system has not been rebuilt, with the result that many parts of the west coast of Newfoundland do not have the privilege of the telegraphic communication they really deserve. Canadian National Telegraphs will say, and have said to me, that when the cost of improving the system is compared with the return it becomes almost a financial impossibility. I agree that in setting up a system of this kind for the west coast of Newfoundland or for any other part of Canada, for that matter, the financial side of the problem must be considered. But on the other hand there is the question of service to people who need it, service that is not too much for any body of people to request in this modern age.
I would hope that we are not too far away from the time when some consideration will be given to the problem. It may well be that if Canadian National Telegraphs is not in a position to institute a service that is able to look after the need of the people, service to these outlying areas could be taken over and operated by the Department of Transport.
A year or so ago a radio station was established at Newcastle, New Brunswick. This radio station was given the same frequency as that of the radio station at Corner Brook in Newfoundland. At the moment the radio
station at Corner Brook cannot be well received in certain parts of the west coast of Newfoundland which for years have been used to the service of this station. The fact that they are not able to receive its programs arises because the local station is being interfered with by the station at Newcastle, New Brunswick, which as I said before is on the same frequency.
I should like to point out that while I make the statement that the station at Newcastle is interfering with the station at Corner Brook, I must recognize the fact that interference is not taking place within the protected area of the station at Newcastle or within the protected area of the station at Corner Brook. But it appears to me that when a station has been given the same frequency as another station and an area which has been accustomed to radio programs from the local station over quite a number of years finds that reception is interfered with, some consideration should be given to the matter.
I have been in touch with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Department of Transport and there is no doubt that these two stations are quite within their legal limits, but here is a section of the Newfoundland coast that is being denied a service which it had for a number of years. I would recommend to the Minister of Transport and the Minister of National Revenue, who speaks for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in parliament, that one of two solutions be adopted; either that the strength of the station CBY at Corner Brook be increased or that the frequency of one of the two stations be changed.
While on the subject I might say that we who live in the Corner Brook area, the second city of Newfoundland, even at this late date are without the services and the pleasures which come from television reception. I mentioned this matter last session to the Minister of National Revenue, and I hope we are not too far away from the time when the microwave line now being constructed across Newfoundland will be completed and a television station established in Corner Brook so those people living in that area-and I number those who would receive television service at about 35,000-.will be able to receive the benefits of television service now enjoyed by such a large proportion of the Canadian population.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a word or two about the trans-Canada highway. It has always been my belief, and it is still my belief, that the trans-Canada highway should have been built across the country entirely by the federal government. If this had been done I believe there would have

The Address-Mr. Belzile
been more equality in the cost of this project, and I particularly refer to the cost to Newfoundland.
The trans-Canada highway, as it was supposed to have been built in my province, would have been built in three stages. There was the first stage of just the rough grading, using material along the right of way the second stage being the strengthening of the subgrade to withstand an axle weight of 18,000 pounds. The material to strengthen the subgrade of a good highway is not very plentiful in Newfoundland and is rather expensive, but this strengthening of the subgrade is a very important part of road construction in a province which has a wide range of moisture and temperature. Furthermore, in the third stage, the paving, we do not have large quantities of the proper aggregate for that sort of work, and many of the materials for paving have to be imported into the province and stored there.
I point out that the project is becoming a very expensive one for my province, not only in the sense that Newfoundland is not an easy province in which to build a highway, but it is expensive also in terms of the amount of road which has to be built by a small population. The total length of the trans-Canada highway is about 4,500 miles. The total length of that highway in Newfoundland is 610 miles, which means that while the population of Newfoundland is only 3.7 per cent of the population of all the provinces which are now under the agreement, yet the proportion of the road which they have to build is 13.3 per cent, roughly three times as much.
We could compare the cost of the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland with the cost in other provinces, for example in Alberta and in Ontario, where the number of miles per 10,000 of population is 2.8. In Manitoba the number of miles per 10,000 population is 3.7. In Saskatchewan the figure is 4.8 miles, in Nova Scotia 4.8, in British Columbia 5.7, in New Brunswick 7.1, in Prince Edward Island 7.3, while in Newfoundland the number of miles per 10,000 of population is 15.8.
I suggest that this project is becoming a most expensive one for a province with a small population and a low tax potential. I would hope that before too long we may be able to hear some discussion on the trans-Canada highway and receive from the government the information that it will be possible to adopt a new approach to a very important problem in Newfoundland, a problem which may be equally important to all the Atlantic provinces.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have the signal honour of rising to speak in this house. I am therefore very pleased to be able to take part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
At the outset, I would like to ask divine Providence to give me the strength, wisdom and knowledge necessary for the proper discharge of the mandate with which I have been entrusted for the greater glory of God and the general interests of my constituency, my province and my country.
I am pleased to extend cordial greetings to my colleagues on both sides of the house. Before coming to the heart of my subject, I would also like to congratulate you, as is proper, on your re-election to the important post you occupy at this time.
I should also like to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) most sincerely for having recently entrusted two portfolios to Quebec members and to congratulate the two new ministers, the hon. members for Lot-biniere (Mr. O'Hurley) and Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) who will be in charge of those departments.
I would feel remiss in my duty were I to ignore the honour which the Prime Minister has conferred on all women by appointing a lady minister to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
Mr. Speaker, on March 31 last, the electors of the constituency of Matapedia-Matane returned me by a considerable majority as their member here. I would like to avail myself of this opportunity to thank them from the bottom of my heart for this high mark of confidence and to assure them of my entire and constant co-operation.
My constituency had been represented since 1935-that is for 23 years-by a Liberal member and, during the last five years of my predecessor's mandate, not once was the voice of Matapedia-Matane heard in this chamber. For five years the name of Matapedia-Matane was not even mentioned in this house. That explains why the constituency of Matapedia-Matane has been neglected by the central government.
Before proceeding any further, Mr. Speaker, I should like, if I may, to describe briefly for the information of hon. members, the geographic situation, the people and the economic conditions of my constituency.
Geographically, the constituency of Matapedia-Matane is at the very gate of the Gaspe peninsula. It comprises the provincial constituency of Matapedia and 18 parishes of the constituency of Matane, including a total of 40 relatively young communities, several

The Address-Mr. Belzile of them not even 50 years old. The climate is fairly rugged, quite cold in winter, ordinarily warm in summer but, unfortunately, the vegetation period is too short. The population of the constituency, numbering approximately 60,000 people, is practically all French speaking. However, we live in close harmony with the few English speaking Canadian families and the few families of Scottish origin.
The people live on agriculture, the lumber industry, the tourist trade and fishing. Gaspe peninsula and the Matapedia valley are a tourist wonderland and the people are affable and hospitable. I take this opportunity of extending to my colleagues, to their relatives and friends, an invitation to visit the Gaspe peninsula and, particularly the constituency of Matapedia-Matane this summer.
And now I take great pleasure in congratulating the government, and in particular the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), for the passing of Bill No. 237, the Agricultural Stabilization Act adopted last January 25.	'
There are two features of this act whose good effects I am very glad to point out, as they concern particularly the farmers and settlers of my constituency. I refer to the support price on butter and the recognition of pulpwood as an agricultural product.
With regard to this last item, I would ask the government to exercise, as soon as possible, the rights conferred to it under section 11 of Bill No. 237. In fact, it is important that the government decide at once the number of cords of wood of a farmer or settler to which the support price would apply, so that the farm prices stabilization board may establish it and see that this legislation is applied as soon as possible.
I should like now to refer to the speech from the throne. I am pleased to note that, in the paragraph concerning unemployment insurance, it is proposed to bring interesting amendments to the legislation. I shall abstain from reading the whole paragraph and, with your permission, I shall read only the last sentence:
Further amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act will be proposed at a later stage in the session.
I was pleased to find this mentioned in the speech from the throne. I would like, therefore, to offer a few suggestions. That legislation has already been amended so as to include fishermen. On the basis of this amendment, I would suggest that all farmers and settlers operating a farm of a cultivated area of less than 50 acres be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits for a period to be determined.

Mr. Speaker, I do not pretend to encyclopaedic knowledge but, as a farmer's son and as a practical farmer myself for close to thirty years, I feel that I have gained some experience as well as some theoretical and especially some practical knowledge in this field. If I urge the government to extend this protection to settlers and young farmers, it is because I realize that people who have enough enterprise, patriotism, courage and determination to settle in a young community on a new land deserve the consideration and encouragement of their leaders.
We are in a period of transition, Mr. Speaker.
There was a time when a settler or young farmer could be sure to find work in the lumber camps in winter, and could then spend the summer, the active farming season, improving his land. But times have changed. This is an age of mechanization and, with the advent of the large caterpillar tractors and trucks, logging companies operate mostly in the summertime, and the young farmer who used to count on the money earned in the bush camps during the winter to improve his farm and equipment, is now forced to earn that money in summer-time and also to rely on unemployment insurance benefits to get over the meager winter and to look after his family.
Under the same heading, Mr. Speaker, there is another aspect of that legislation which is harmful to the farmers of all countries. At the present time, farm workers are uneligible for insurance, whether they work at the construction or repair of farm buildings, or cut wood on farm wood lots. This is unfair not only to the farmer, but to the worker as well who, by taking on a seasonal job on the farm, is deprived of unemployment insurance benefits during the off-season.
Many of my electors wrote me about this, and I would like to be permitted to quote from one of the letters I have received. Recently a farmer in my riding wrote to an unemployment insurance office in the district, asking if insurance was available to a farm hand in his employ. On May 8 last, the office concerned, that is the one in Rimouski, wrote to him as follows:
Sir,
Re your letter of May 5, 1958.
People hired by a farmer on work connected with agriculture such as seeding, harvesting, wood cutting, and so on, are not insurable and no contribution is required.
In that case, Mr. Speaker, an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act would be a boon to the farmers who would have no trouble finding farm labour if these

The Address-Mr. Belzile
people, knowing that their job is insurable, could count on receiving the benefits during the off-season.
Another federal government agency which could be improved is the farm loan board. In my humble opinion, the $10,000 ceiling on loans is too low. How is it that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation can grant loans of $8,000 to $9,000 on houses that do not cost more than $10,000 or $11,000? Farm houses of equal or even greater value, are not rare and, moreover, the farm includes other buildings and some 75 to 100 acres of cultivated land.
Some would even say that there is an anomaly between the loans granted by the two agencies and the value of a property guaranteeing the loan. I therefore suggest to the government that the maximum loan granted to a farmer be raised from $10,000 to $15,000, provided the farmer offers adequate collateral.
I also take pleasure in congratulating the government for the legislation enacted during the 23rd parliament to improve our system of social security in Canada. And, since it seems obvious that it is the central government's responsibility to help the young generation in the field of education, in my humble opinion we already have on our statute books legislation specially suited to that purpose, and I refer to the Family Allowances Act.
In the first place, they should be raised proportionately to the present cost of living as compared with the cost of living at the time they were first introduced. Secondly, they should be paid until children who are still attending school reach their 18th year.
Before concluding these remarks, may I be allowed to point out to hon. members that the area commonly called the Matapedia and Gaspe valley is part of Canada, that the people of this vast and recent section of the country pay taxes to the federal government and contribute to the building up of our homeland, and therefore are entitled to consideration on the part of the federal government.
It is an area that was very much neglected by the former administration which now, fortunately, is sitting on the other side of the house.
In the field of public works, I strongly support the proposal of my colleague, the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. English), who wants to provide for the extension of the Mont Joli-Matane railroad to Ste. Anne des Monts.
The harbour of the town of Matane is a wonderful site for a winter port. If that harbour were developed, and a ferry service put in to ensure regular communication between Matane on the south shore and Baie
Comeau or Seven Islands on the north shore, it would be of great economic assistance to the area and would make it much easier for farmers on the south shore to market their produce in the large manufacturing towns on the north shore. In addition, it would provide local employment to large numbers of workers in and around Matane.
Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned earlier in my remarks, the growing season is rather short in the Matapedia valley and Gaspe. Specialized farming, such as fruit farming, truck farming et cetera, is out of the question. On the whole, it is an area of general or mixed farming. Our basic farm products are butter and related products. Our farmers' cash income is derived from dairy products, mainly butter, cattle, butcher hogs and poultry.
Most communities being far removed from large cities, we have to ship our products to the larger markets.
I wonder whether there is not here a case of utter economic nonsense. While farmers in the Matapedia valley and in Matane riding are only 30 miles away, across the St. Lawrence, from large north shore centres like Forestviile, Labrieville, Baie Comeau, Haute-rive, Seven Islands and Shefferville, where not a single vegetable can be grown, people in those large centres have to order their food products from the large markets of Quebec and Montreal. This illogical situation exists because the producer has to pay too high a price for the transport of his produce to the large markets in Quebec and Montreal, over and above costs of handling, and then has to ship it back down the St. Lawrence, or by air for consumption on our doorstep, that is, 30 miles away from home on the north shore. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I favour this project to organize, for the benefit of people on the south shore, some service to promote the sale of our home products on markets that are practically on our threshold and which are logically ours.
I also would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) on an essential service which affects the people in my riding. I refer to telephone service. During the winter months, our local climate is severe. A number of farmers and settlers live several miles away from their common business centre and, moreover, several parishes have no resident physician. In case of urgent illness and hospitalization, a telephone service would greatly help alleviate suffering and even save some lives.
There has been legislation adopted for the protection of animals but I repeat that in certain circumstances, in some of our parish concessions, many human lives are not adequately protected.

I feel sure that during this session and subsequent ones, I will have an opportunity to return in more detail to the ideas which I have just put forward.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an urgent appeal to all my colleagues from the province of Quebec, even to those who sit in the opposition. I would like them to join with the other members of the Canadian provinces in a common effort, and following the example of the Prime Minister, in whose person are exemplified good understanding, harmony and unity, to bring to the service of our country a spirit of co-operation.
Mr. Speaker, once again, I say that the time of racial and religious prejudices has gone. I would ask every hon. member of this house, whatever his race or his religion to unite in a common effort and, in a fine gesture of national unity, to work for the full development of this country of ours, Canada.

Most hon. members have a feeling that their own electoral district is, as it were, a miniature Canada. The constituency of Brome-Missisquoi is no exception. It includes Canadians whose ancestors were of French, English, Polish, Japanese, Italian and other origins. They work in plants or on the farm. Others operate businesses, large or small. However, Mr. Speaker, the most important point is that there are, in my riding, citizens of the two great races that contribute to a truly Canadian culture and which, moreover, give our great and young country, Canada, its strength and glory.
Since I have been in politics, I have always done my best to preserve the spirit of patriotism which inspired Cartier and Macdonald. This I have always done with determination and sincerity.
(Text):
Canada, Mr. Speaker, was built on the spirit of Cartier and Macdonald. Today this spirit recognizes that not only Canadians whose traditions go back to England and France form our great country, but that Canadians whose heritages go back to many lands all over the world form the glory and force of Canada. The people of Brome-Missisquoi recognize this, and I speak in this chamber with great emotion and sincerity when I say that, practically for the first time in the history of Canada, a young man has been elected to this house, with English as his mother tongue, by an electorate largely made up of French speaking Canadians.
On March 31 last confederation became a realization. Real national unity is now a fact, and I can inform all members of the opposi-

tion that the divide and rule game is over both in Brome-Missisquoi and in the province of Quebec. The people of my area and my province will no longer tolerate sectional appeals. In past years far too many men in public life have come into the province of Quebec with one program for Canada and yet another for our province; but under the leadership of the Prime Minister the Progressive Conservative party presented one united program for all Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
I was most interested in the remarks made by one of the members from Alberta and one of the members from Ontario. The same spirit of pan-Canadianism which brought our party into force and into being in the province of Ontario had exactly the same effect in my province. Our party came into Quebec with dignity and force.
I should like to thank the people of Brome-Missisquoi for the support they gave me on March 31 last. In backing the present government my people rejoiced in the fact that taxes were lowered while at last the rights of the old people have been fully recognized. They rejoice in the fact that the eastern farmers will finally have a voice on the federal level. I believe most hon. members recognize that during past years the revenue of the eastern farmer has gone down while his expenses have gone up.
The textile industry has noted with much pleasure that immediate action is pending in order to halt unfair dumping practices. The government proposal to create an agency for small business is more than welcomed by the small businessman in the district, the businessman who has suffered under past credit restrictions. Federal action with regard to a national hospital and health plan will benefit my people more than I can say. In my tours about Brome-Missisquoi I noted a feeling amongst the people that they are being saddled with hospital bills that just could not be met. My people feel, Mr. Speaker, that legislation of this kind to enable citizens to pay hospital bills cannot come any to soon.
Government action with regard to housing is helping more Canadians buy their own homes. I submit that any legislation which recognizes the integrity of the family unit, as this does, is more than welcome in my area just as it is welcome in many areas throughout the country. I sincerely hope that under
The Address-Mr. Grafftey this new legislation that we recently passed, money for building new homes will find its way into rural areas. During past years my constituents have had some difficulty in securing loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I feel certain that in the very near future these loans will be readily available.
Labour welcomes recent unemployment insurance legislation, and at the same time appreciates the fact the workingman is being given increased representation on government boards. I believe that my area is not unlike many similar areas in its attitude toward government departments such as the departments of public works and defence production. My electors feel that whenever it is administratively possible and practicable, decentralized buying and contract-letting policies should be carried out. So long as the citizen's tax dollar is being most economically handled, we should stress a program of local work for local people. In other words, fairly justifiable objections are heard when large city firms enter rural ridings to undertake contracts or to carry out works which rural people feel they could do at a cheaper rate themselves.
Personally I welcome the announced intention of the justice department concerning the old ticket of leave regulations. Penal reforms' are so necesary in Canada, and I believe that any dollar spent on increased psychiatric, probation or parole services by the Department of Justice is worth a thousand dollars spent on any high-wall prison. I welcome also the reference to that department's effort to define the word "obscenity". I look forward, as I am sure many hon. members look forward, to the day when the young people of our country can be protected from the yellow scandal sheets which are being passed about from coast to coast.
I sincerely hope my hon. friends of the C.C.F. note that all the above-mentioned legislation recognizes the welfare of all Canadians. It is legislation which recognizes that we are individuals with diverse aspirations. We lay no claim to a monopoly on concern for our fellowmen; yet, unlike contemporary socialist doctrine, our legislative ambitions do not intend to dragoon Canadians in the name of uniformity.

This is as it should be, for the voice of the people is our strength.

It has always been my belief that our greatest contribution to international order should be based on an understanding and policy of enlightened nationalism which, in turn, accentuates the true meaning of international interdependence. Such interdependence underlies the


basic facts of modern international existence. The very statesmanship that our party, and all other parties, has exerted in solidifying the bonds of our own confederation offers us a glorious chance to push forward our influence in the world of 1958.

Thus, while a new Canadianism will speak in a frank and friendly way to the United States and to the United Kingdom, the quality of our contribution to world order lies in our ability to interpret the old world to the new and the new to the old, while explaining our own stand in clear and unmistakable terms. Mr. Speaker, first I should like to add my congratulations to those of others who have spoken upon your reappointment. I should like to extend congratulations also to the Deputy Speaker. Personally I am very happy with the choice of Speaker. The job he did in the last parliament when there was a minority government was a credit to him and I think was largely responsible for the kind words that have been said about him and the support he received for his renomination. Because of the imbalance of membership in the House of Commons now I think he is going to have a continuing problem. Not only is he going to have to be the referee but also the spokesman for and supporter of the minority groups in the house, a position I am sure he is quite capable of filling.
With the present imbalance of membership in the House of Commons I think now would be an exceptionally good time for us to take a look at the need to have a permanent Speaker. I know there are many problems involved, but other countries have surmounted them and they are not problems that cannot be surmounted. One qualification the present Speaker has that would be an advantage if the office were made permanent is his ability, I am told, to speak flawless French. I think

it is most necessary that we keep politics out of the choosing of a permanent Speaker. The office is that of a referee who cannot take sides; therefore I think we would have to consider several methods of electing the man we would choose as permanent Speaker of the House of Commons.
I suggest that there are several ways this could be done. Some of them have been discussed before, but as government members have advocated this move on a number of occasions in the past I think they are now in a position to carry it out. I would suggest that one method would be to set up an independent constituency consisting of the members of parliament who constitute the House of Commons. They could then elect the Speaker immediately preceding dissolution, when they would actually be endorsing the Speaker they had had. This would eliminate some of the faults that would be inherent if they chose him immediately after an election. Again, we could follow the system used in Great Britain, where by agreement among the political parties the Speaker is given an acclamation in a particular riding. However, in Canada we have a multi-party system, and on many occasions we have seen independent candidates nominated. I do not believe we could assure the Speaker that he would always be unopposed and therefore receive an acclamation.
I think there is a great deal to be said in favour of making a permanent appointment, but the idea also has some faults. With a permanent appointment we might find the same faults that I think many of us felt were a problem with regard to the gentleman we were told this morning we were not supposed to refer to. I refer to the fact that his appointment was not strictly in accordance with the procedure that had been followed in the past. I think if it were done on that basis problems might develop because of those who had appointed the particular gentleman. I believe the house should consider and discuss the question of the appointment of a permanent Speaker for the House of Commons.
In the present parliament there are probably more young people than the House of Commons has seen for years. In my opinion this is a very good thing for Canada. It shows that young people are taking an interest in politics, and having listened to their speeches we are quite well aware that most of them are very capable. I think it is time,
The Address-Mr. Peters certainly after the debate on the speech from the throne is over, to start enforcing the rule against the reading of speeches, because by that time most of the new members will have made their maiden speeches. Certainly those I have heard speak so far are quite capable of making their own speeches without reading them. I believe they should do so; say what they want to say, represent the people who sent them here, and not read speeches that sound really nice but have been put down on paper by someone else with no interest in the particular riding and the ideas the new member may have. I do not think parliament was meant to be a place for the reading of speeches, and I believe the rule should be enforced so that members will speak of what they know concerning conditions in their own ridings, and do so to the best of their ability.
There is another development which may be a good one. I have noticed in the newspapers that no parliamentary assistants have been reappointed this year. Inasmuch as we have been able to get along without them for a few months I think it may be quite possible that we can do without them entirely. I say this because the government has so many followers that if it rewards all those who are justly deserving we will have so many parliamentary assistants and secretaries to parliamentary assistants that the administration wjll be top heavy. Inasmuch as the government has not appointed any so far and we have got along fine, I believe it might be advisable not to bother appointing any parliamentary assistants for this session and see how things go. I realize that there must be some training in order to rise to the ministerial level, but possibly that could be spread around among two or three people for each department.
I have been amused this session by the introduction into the debate a great number of times of the name of Maurice Duplessis. I come from Ontario, and I am neither for nor against this. I have certain ideas I have mentioned a number of . times in connection with particular matters in which I am interested but what amuses me is the fact that I believe it is generally assumed that Maurice Duplessis supports those people who have been elected from Quebec. For a long time we heard the Conservatives crying about the fact that this machine in Quebec was working for the election of the Liberals, and now we hear the Liberals crying just as hard that the machine is working for the election of the Conservatives. If this gentleman wants to get into politic; federally I suggest he should campaign

The Address-Mr. Peters federally and bring his machine with him, because it may produce some very unusual results.

I am not particularly impressed by one group saying, now that the tide has turned, that Maurice Duplessis is a terrible man and that the results he will produce will be bad, when I have heard the same thing from the other side. Coming from Ontario perhaps I might say that his influence cannot be very good no matter which side it is on.
As a member from northern Ontario I have been most interested in the extensive remarks made by a number of speakers with regard to the vision of the Prime Minister. In northern Ontario we have often seen visions but they are not mirages. These are known as the aurora borealis, more commonly known as the northern lights. In my part of the country they pass so close that many times you can hear them, and we are very impressed by them. Canadian scientists are interested in developing some of the potential of the northern lights.
For years the people of northern Ontario have been interested in the development of that region, and we are now passing into a new phase where if we do not do something the development that started 50 or 60 years ago is going to come to naught. About 60 or 65 years ago the pioneers came to northern Ontario and opened up the northland. My father was one of those pioneers who at that time and as a very young boy came into northern Ontario. These people came in and bought the land where only a few years before the first white men had arrived in a country which had some of the most beautiful white pine in Canada. They arrived in this area, cut trees, cleared the land, created the farms, until now in Timiskaming we have one of the nicest farming areas in Ontario. They developed the farms and produced an exceptional quantity and quality of produce and now we find out of 1,600 such farms containing taxable farm land, only 400 of them support families engaged in agriculture. Yes, they did their share; they undertook the development of northern Ontario and they pioneered, but what have the governments done to assist them in the meantime?
A number of years ago the government of Ontario had one of these big development visions that we hear so much about. They put in a railway for the development of northern Ontario, and they called it Ontario's development road. This railway stretches from North Bay right through to James bay, Moose Factory being the northern terminal. It was put through not necessarily to make a profit but to help the people of northern

Ontario by providing an opportunity for bringing in supplies and taking out produce. As the years went by this railway, which unlike many railways has supplied a service to the people has become more interested in showing a nice profit at the end of the year.
I am afraid that when the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen)-for whom I have a great deal of sympathy, and I think anyone would have sympathy with a person who had three elections in the space of eight or nine months-finds that all this development is not going to happen simply because of a vision, and that the development of the Yukon will not take place immediately, he will be very disillusioned. We were told all that in northern Ontario, and I am afraid he will find the same situation that we found.
There was another road through northern Ontario which was going to be a development road; I refer to the Canadian National railway line put through from Quebec to the west, passing through the town of Cochrane. This line is owned by the Canadian people; they paid for it, and they were supposed to have bought this railway from a lot of bankrupt companies a long time ago. I am no economist; I do not pretend to be one, nor do I want to be one, but I read in the paper yesterday that the C.N.R. has a deficit of $29,600,000. The article goes on to say that it is true they made a profit of $7J million, but the debt interest amounted to something like $37 million.
Are the people of Canada not sufficiently adult to know or to realize that if we have bought this railroad we want to own it. For goodness sake let us pay for it and get rid of this debt. I see no reason why we should be told this railway is losing money when we did not bother to make payment for that railway so that it now shows a charge to the railway of a debt interest of $37 million.

I think it is time we did something about paying for this railroad-we thought we had bought it-and we should not turn for our tax structure to the C.P.R. but rather to the railroad we own ourselves and should know therefore how it is being operated. We should discuss tariffs and other matters which are connected with railways and the development of our country. I do not think we are going- to be able to do all this as long as we have this large sum of money sitting there on which we are paying interest. I agree that we bought it, and bought it at a fantastic price. Now let us take the money from one pocket and pay off this debt so we can accumulate all our debts in the one

place and we do not have to show a large amount of interest on every balance sheet.
The town of Cochrane is a very important town so far as this railway is concerned. It is the junction of the Canadian National northern branch and the Ontario Northland Railway, and is completely dependent on the C.N.R. It was built for that purpose; it functions as a junction point and as a district office for that railway. Now we find that the people are no longer interested in maintaining Cochrane as a railway town, but for some queer reason-and I suspect perhaps Mr. Duplessis comes back into the issue here- they want to move the railroad divisional point and shops down to Senneterre. Senne-terre has no buildings which are suitable for railway shops, it has no jack or grinder, but that is where they are going to move the shops.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment I was mentioning the fact that the shops of the Canadian National Railways in Cochrane were being moved to Senneterre in the province of Quebec. As I pointed out, this town has been completely dependent for its livelihood on the railroad and on railroad operations. Cochrane is a town of about 3,000 people supported by the workers who were told only a few weeks ago that they would have to move. The other day I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) a question about it, and he referred it to the officials of the C.N.R. What has been said by their officials has been said many times by the Canadian National Railways, and it goes something like this: all the problams that we face, whether labour problems or anything else, are tied to automation; we cannot hold up progress; we cannot do what you ask, because automation has made it more economical to do something else.
Well, we are financing the Canadian National Railways and I think we should decide what we are going to do about its operations. When this line was put into northern Ontario it was a development line intended to help open up the north. This development is still necessary, because it has never been completed. It is my opinion that since we are helping to finance this line we should at least maintain those towns which were built up for the purpose of northern development. One of the company's officials wrote to me a day or two ago about this move to Senneterre.
The Address-Mr. Peters
I have visited the shops in Cochrane and have verified for myself several things which were pointed out to me there. It was pointed out that these shops were already partly converted to diesel operations; that they had 18 stalls for engines, and a well-equipped engine shed, the west end of which had already been converted. For five years the shop has serviced all the diesels and equipment operating in that division and the division in Quebec. It is servicing now 20 units a month and with very little additional expenditure these facilities could service 40 engines, more than are required in that area. To complete the modernization of the roundhouse would cost a very small sum of money, but it is estimated it would cost about $1 million to build a new shop in Senneterre. This would represent $1 million more to be added to the loss which Canadian National is now incurring, in addition to these people being asked to move into a town which has no housing, no suitable schools and no facilities in general for their reception. They are being asked to leave a place in which they have lived for many years, the reason given being that a new line has been built north into Chibougamau. I think anyone who has studied the financial papers during the last year will appreciate that if there is no change in the base price for copper that line will not be of much value to anybody. If copper prices fall much further the tracks will be rusting before much time has passed.
That is not true of Cochrane. Cochrane could serve both east and west. In addition, if further railway facilities should be required one of the most modern diesel shops in all Canada, operated by the Ontario Northland railway, is situated in the town, and if the C.N.R. requires additional facilities there is no reason why they should not make use of these.
I am also informed that the railway service given to this area west of Hearst is, to say the least, lousy. The company operates one small car, and part of that car is a baggage car. I suggest that if the officials of Canadian National do not wish to operate this railway as a railway it should sell the line to the O.N.R. which would at least give service even if it did sacrifice development for profit.
I think this question of railroads is of the utmost importance to the people of northern Ontario and I agree with the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) that it is also of the utmost importance to the rest of Canada. But merely to put in these development lines is not enough; we must be prepared to do something for the people who develop the areas into which we put the railroads. Simply to run a track through there is not good

The Address-Mr. Peters enough. These people built up those areas and gave their life's blood to do it, and then they find that support is suddenly taken from under them.
We who come from northern Ontario, and particularly from Timiskaming where we have the largest gold mine in North America, were very interested in the item in the speech from the throne which related to the emergency gold mining assistance program. Hon. members who sit on the Conservative benches today are probably more familiar than any other group of people with the needs and requirements of the gold mining industry. In the past many able spokesmen for the gold mining industry have sat on the Conservative benches of the House of Commons, and I am quite sure that they are giving consideration to this matter at the present time.
I think they would agree with me when I say that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act is not in itself, nor ever has been, an answer to the problem which faces the gold mine operators and the communities dependent on these operations. What we need is a more realistic price for the product we are marketing. I hold no brief for the mining industry. This industry has in the past abused its workers, refused in many cases to give consideration to the communities which have grown up around it, and behaved in dictatorial fashion in its relations with its labour force-a fact which I have personally experienced in the picket lines on a number of occasions. Nevertheless, it is true that costs in the industry have increased and it is also true that the price of gold has remained stable. For these reasons I make a plea that the government should at least continue to operate the emergency gold mining assistance measure.
Some time ago the gold mining communities across Canada prepared a brief which they presented to the government. I think each hon. member has received a copy of this submission. It was started by the town of Timmins and some of the other municipalities, and intended to make a case, not for the gold mining industry or for the workers engaged in it but rather for the communities and municipalities dependent on that industry, because those communities have reached the position where they can no longer look ahead with confidence but must count themselves lucky if they are able to keep the ground they have already gained. They pointed out in this brief that one of the most important and immediate things to be done if the communities dependent on gold mining are to continue to grow is to eliminate the word "emergency" from this act. It is true that when the prices of everything first began

to rise an emergency developed in the gold mining industry. The subsidy provided under the act could at that time be described legitimately as meeting an emergency. But the situation which the subsidy was designed to meet does not appear to be coming to an end, and we think the least that could be done now would be to take the word "emergency" out of the title so that the communities to which I refer might have something they can look forward to year after year.
We all agree that this act is no solution to the question. We think the Canadian people should press very hard for an increase in the price of gold. This may mean, if we are unable to have any change made in the international monetary system, that the Canadian people themselves should buy gold at a higher price than they are now doing. I could go into all the faults of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act; I could point out that we find gold mines low grading their mines so that they are making more money out of the subsidy than out of their mining operations, continually hoping that one day the price of gold will rise and they will be able to take advantage of the increased price. I could point out all the problems that are developing in the industry, but I think they are fairly well known to the Canadian people. They know that this industry has been one of the major reasons why northern Ontario developed, and that some consideration must be given to it. In the developments which are planned for the future we are going to find in our northland increased wealth of all kinds.
If we are not willing to do something for the people in northern Ontario why should the people in areas that have not yet been scratched hope that conditions are going to be better for them? Northern Ontario has reached a stage in its existence at which secondary industries must be encouraged to locate there if it is going to continue to develop from the point it has now reached. In order to accomplish this the assistance of the provincial and federal governments will be required. The brief to which I have referred was prepared by William Lougheed Associates, consulting economists of Toronto, in April 1958. At page 93 the following statement appears:
What is required is something more than hard work, optimistic talk, and detailed planning. That something consists essentially of potential markets, for without them productive potential means nothing . . . But if the northland is to rescue the goldmining communities, they will have to survive until northern promise comes to fruition. As in the case of underwriting gold, then, the subsidizing of economic diversification is essentially a play for time.

Diversification can come about only if the governments are willing to encourage secondary industries to locate in northern Ontario. I believe that the economic attaches visiting Canada from other countries must be looking for communities similar to those in northern Ontario. Surely there is a department of government which can get in touch with these communities and supply them with the contacts that are necessary for bringing in secondary industries. If the railroads and the highways are still for the purpose of development then they can be subsidized. Some of the profit from the railways serving that area could be used to establish and attract secondary industries. The municipalities have indicated their willingness to do something to meet the problem and I only suggest that the federal government should fulfil some of its promises by establishing secondary industries in this area which has already witnessed a degree of development before opening new areas.
I have in my hand a compilation of information concerning communities in northern Ontario and I propose to take my home community of New Liskeard as just one example. It is indicated in this booklet that New Liskeard is located in the district of Timiskaming and is serviced by the Ontario Northland railway, Walter Little transport, highway No. 11, and has an airport at Earlton, 20 miles distant. It has a population of approximately 4,600 and it is noted with regard to housing that present construction meets demands. It has a labour force of 3,000 within a 25-mile radius and it is indicated that industrial sites are available with areas zoned for industry. The potential market for consumer goods is also set out in this publication. Similar information is available for many other communities in northern Ontario. I urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) to arrange to put these communities which are in need of secondary industry in touch with the appropriate people who could meet that need. The potential consumer market of 500,000 people is not great in relation to that of southern Ontario but this district could support many small plants employing between 40 and 50 men. The district has both the necessary raw materials and the facilities and is eager to put them at the disposal of secondary industries.
One of the problems in the development of the north is the matter of highway transport. A great deal has been said concerning necessary safety measures on the railways.
I investigated some of these statements and rode in a number of train engine cabs and noticed the differences in diesel engines.
57071-3-274
The Address-Mr. Peters The unions concerned have indicated that safety is a problem. The Canadian people were told by the railways that if the engineer died a dead man control would go on under certain circumstances. In the course of investigating an engine in Cochrane I observed that the dead man control in one particular type of engine was in the form of a long bar around the seat of the cab. No matter where the engineer might fall if he were taken ill or if he were to die his body would strike the bar and the dead man control would not go on and the train would continue for some distance. I asked the engineer how far the train would go under those circumstances and he said that unless something else happened to stop it the engine carried enough oil that it could travel from Cochrane to Montreal. It is obvious that a dead man control is not much of a safety factor.
The hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) and I rode in the cab of an engine on the Canadian National Railways main line at North Bay. In the cab in question we discovered you could press the dead man control down and it would remain depressed until you gave it a kick and brought it up again.
I did not conduct an extensive investigation but it brought some interesting facts to light.
If there is a safety question on the railways there is an even greater and more important one with regard to highway transport. The highway in northern Ontario is an alternative route to the west. It is the only trans-Canada highway and it is a matter to which I hope consideration will be given. After we get No. 17 highway through I hope the government will still see fit to call No. 11 a second trans-Canada highway. Some consideration should be given by the Department of Transport to trucks travelling through that area. Some drivers travel for 50 or 60 hours at a time without relief. In a condition of fatigue a driver is a menace regardless of how skilled he is.
Another matter that should be brought into the open is that of the railways owning and competing with themselves in highway transport. You and I are asked to subsidize these companies. I believe it is necessary to have at least two people in the cab of an engine on a train at all times and it is equally essential that there be two people in the cab of a transport truck. They should not be permitted to work without relief for excessive periods of time because you and I are going to meet these trucks on the highway and personally I would just as soon meet a truck driver who is wide awake than one who has one eye closed when he is in charge of his vehicle. These matters should be discussed and regulations brought in to control them. At this time

Although my time has nearly expired I wish to mention the trans-Canada pipeline. Doubtless we will be afforded an opportunity of discussing this on another occasion. I believe that many hon. members who participate in the debates of this house in the next few months, if they are honest, are going to press strongly for the bringing of this pipeline under government control. Mr. Speaker, my first words in this debate are to associate myself with the words of congratulations from the other speakers to you, sir, on your re-appointment to the chair, to the Deputy Speaker and to the other officers of this House of Commons, and to the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
In speaking on the motion of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech from the throne I would like to ask the indulgence of this house to recapitulate briefly the accomplishments of the Progressive Conservative government since June 10, particularly as they apply to my province of Newfoundland and to my constituency.
It has been said, in Newfoundland, particularly during the election campaign and prior to that campaign, that the Progressive Conservative government has done a great deal for Newfoundland to correct some of the inadequacies and the shortcomings that befell my province upon our entry into confederation in 1949. The record is plain for all to see. For example, since June 10, the long-awaited, badly needed St. John's harbour development has become a reality. This multi-million dollar development to the old historic port of St. John's, the most easterly harbour in Canada, will do much for my city toward lowering the cost of freight handling


and thereby contribute greatly to a general reduction in what is now one of the highest cost of living in Canada. This development it is true, will also result in the creation of many jobs for the people in my constituency and it comes as a welcome sign, particularly with the pending reduction of the United States armed forces in eastern Newfoundland.
Secondly, what I consider to be one of the more important achievements of the Progressive Conservative government, as it applies to my province and indeed to Canada, is the realistic approach to the housing problems of this country. It has been said earlier in this debate that nothing contributes so much to the local economy of an area as a general boom in house-building. This government, realizing the relative importance of low-cost housing to Canadians, and realizing the jobs that will be created from housing developments generally, have tackled this problem generously and realistically. The result of that realistic approach to housing will mean that in this coming year in the city of St. John's house-building will be more than double what it was last year.
I am particularly pleased, as I am sure other Newfoundland members in this House of Commons are, to see in the estimates for the coming fiscal year provision for a modern car ferry to operate between the mining town of Bell island in my constituency and the local mainland. This long overdue car ferry was denied the people of Newfoundland for eight long years, until it became practically a political football. It was handed back from the provincial government to the federal government to the provincial government, and nobody wanted to tackle this problem. But now the people of Bell island, who contribute so much to the economy of Newfoundland and indeed to eastern Canada, with one of the largest deposits of iron ore in North America, are to have at long last an adequate car ferry to provide adequate and proper communication between Bell Island and the local mainland.
There is also in the estimates for this year -and no doubt hon. members opposite will also appreciate the relative importance of those expenditures-provision for the erection of new dock facilities and new warehouse facilities for Bell island, which has a population, I might add, of some 12,000 souls, thereby enabling the people of Bell island to have their supplies, their provisions and their goods shipped direct, thereby again reducing a far too high cost of living. This is the realistic way in which the Progressive Conservative government approaches the long unsolved problems of the Atlantic provinces generally. Of course, the increases in old

age pensions and social security benefits generally are by no means unwelcome in Newfoundland because I am sure hon. members will realize that the people of Newfoundland were blinded by the promise of social security benefits and old age pensions until it practically reached the stage where this was the sum total of being a Canadian. But, as I have found out, there is much more to belonging to this great nation than old age security and family allowances.
I also think it is ironic that those increases should come from a Conservative government. We are all familiar with the old cry that was spread east and west and north and south in Newfoundland-and I believe on the mainland of Canada-that if you vote for the Tories you lose your old age pension and your baby bonus.

and congratulations to the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of this house. I wish also to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for their very able presentations.
It gives me a great deal of pleasure and I feel it is a privilege to represent the constituency of Acadia in this house because this constituency has never been represented in parliament on the side of the government and has never before been represented by a Conservative. Bearing this in mind I trust the hon. ministers will not be too greatly perturbed at me for trying to better conditions in Acadia.
Acadia is a large constituency approximately 200 miles square located in the east central part of Alberta. In the northwestern part we have a mixed farming area and in the vicinity of the town of Stettler a large oil development. Throughout the whole constituency there are vast reserves of natural gas. In the southern part there are some very good farming and ranching areas. The constituency is bounded on the south and southwest by the Red Deer river and I might at this time point out that along this river, stretching from Drumheller through the town of Buffalo a distance of 150 miles, we have no bridge. This fact brings great hardship to the people on both sides of the river in the spring and fall when the ferries are not running.
Another unique problem in this constituency is that it is entirely rural. It consists mainly of farming and ranching areas and although the farmers and ranchers may not be the best in Canada they are some of the best people in the country and I am honoured to represent them in this house.
On first hearing the speech from the throne I was surprised and pleased to learn of the work and action intended by this government. Since the opening of parliament I have listened with a great deal of patience to the opposition criticizing the government for no action to aid the economic situation in this country, and with the next breath saying that the speech from the throne is the longest and contains the most legislation that they have ever heard. The speech from the throne outlines a great deal of work that will benefit my constituency. The bill of rights is something that will benefit all Canadians. The extension of the unemployment assistance, which has already come to pass, will be of great aid to the unemployed, since it will give them an additional six weeks to find employment.
The house-building industry has already received additional aid which will benefit the country and create more employment. At

this time I might point out that the authorities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should be advised to be more careful when it comes to making loans in what they describe as partially restricted areas, because in some of the smaller towns in Canada a loan for house construction means as much for the welfare of the citizens as it does in the larger cities.
I was pleased to note that, according to the speech from the throne, work will be started on the South Saskatchewan river dam. Probably a great number of members from Saskatchewan will be surprised to learn that this should interest me. This action proves to me that there is still hope for the Red Deer river diversion scheme in Alberta. While it is a fact that the South Saskatchewan river dam will no doubt limit the size of the Red Deer river project, yet it shows me that when we have a government in Alberta that is willing to go ahead and develop this part of Alberta we might receive some consideration from this government.
I was pleased to note in the speech from the throne that there is work to be done in deepening the harbours of Port Arthur and Fort William. This will no doubt lower the cost of grain movement and thereby benefit the farmers of western Canada.
An amendment to the act having to do with cash advances is included in the speech from the throne. That legislation was very much disputed in this house. While the Conservative party was in opposition it advocated cash advances. The Liberals said at that time that it could not be done. After this government came into office last year cash advances were put into effect and now, after learning from the experience gained since the enacting of the measure, we see where we can amend it so it will be even more beneficial to the farmers in the west.
I am vitally interested in the amendment proposed to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The constituency of Acadia has always received some assistance under this act, but there have always been some injustices. In the past few years very little wheat has been grown in parts of my constituency and because of this farmers have been declared ineligible. While we have this surplus wheat problem I think the farmers who are not growing wheat should be praised and not punished. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act is a type of insurance against drought, hail and other hazards. We all know, that such hazards as hail and drought do not travel in a straight line or confine themselves to blocks in townships. The act should be amended to make it more suitable for the type of conditions it is to cover.
