But the offer was most sincere and the offer was always there;
Newfoundland has changed her mind, and in time she too may find
Burdens shared are light to bear, triumphs shared are double dear,
She has gladly joined the sheaf bounded by the maple leaf;
Knowing well she still may boast answering in her sister's toast;
But Newfoundland was proud to be England's oldest colony.

At the present time Newfoundland is anxiously awaiting the report of the royal commission on term 29 of our entry into confederation with the nine provinces of Canada. The district I have the honour to represent contains some of the oldest occupied parts of the new world. Its shores were the scene of some of the oldest commercial activity in North America. It was in Cupids in Conception bay that John Guy of Bristol started a colony at the same time the first English settlement on the mainland was started at Jamestown, Virginia. British firms established branches at a very early date in Trinity. Although these original businesses have disappeared, the main industry which attracted commercial adventurers to this remote area continues to flourish in Trinity and Conception bays.
My district is made up of approximately 180 communities with a population of 57,000 inhabitants. There are many settlements in my riding with lovely names. Here are a few which might be of interest to this house: Little Heart's Ease, Heart's Delight, Heart's Desire, Heart's Content, where the S.S. Great Eastern landed the first transatlantic cable. We also have the following places: British Harbour, Ireland's Eye, Whiterock, Flatrock, Caplin Cove, Burnt Point, Lead Cove, Chapel Arm, Bay-de-Verde, Freshwater, Blow-me-Down, Blackhead, Dough Fig Point, Hatchet Cove and Come-by-Chance. The riding begins at Spillar's Cove just a mile south of cape Bonavista, where John Cabot discovered the new world, and takes in Trinity and Conception bays, ending at Georgetown near Brigus, the home of the late Captain Bob Bartlett, the famous arctic explorer.
Some of the most modern fish plants in eastern Canada are within the confines of my riding. There is a large fresh fish plant at Harbour Grace, which is owned by NorthEastern Fisheries Ltd. At Dildo there is a large whaling and fresh fish operation, and here an extension to the wharf is badly needed. At Catalina in the northerly part of my riding is probably the greatest concentration of fresh fish plants in eastern Canada. This is the headquarters of the huge Fishermen's Union Trading Company which has a great supply business and salt fish processing plant at Port Union, which is also the headquarters of the Union Electric Light and Power Company and the home of the newspaper, the Fisherman's Advocate. From the harbour of Catalina is exported approximately one-quarter of all Newfoundland salt codfish.
In the same harbour there is also a large modern fresh fish plant belonging to Fishery Products Limited. This plant, which is one
The Address-Mr. Tucker of the largest frozen fish plants in Newfoundland, has just been completed. Also in Catalina harbour in the northwest arm is a large federal experimental salt fish drier located in the premises of S. W. Mifflin Limited. This plant, the most modern of its kind, is proving that light salted shore fish can be cured artificially and economically. I am pleased to say that during recent years the Liberal government, by means of an enlightened dredging program, improved the harbour of Catalina making it more feasible to carry on business. A coastal wharf is also being built and is situated in the most sheltered part of the harbour. I am also very happy to say that Little Catalina, a large settlement devoted almost wholly to the production of salt fish, will soon have a breakwater which will greatly facilitate the fishermen in their vocation. At Elliston, approximately ten miles north of Catalina, is located another fish plant. There are a number of other places in the riding where public works would prove of great economic benefit and I shall deal with those as time goes on and with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green).
Clarenville on Trinity bay is a rail centre and a distribution point for supplies. Clarenville became world famous in 1935 as the place where General Balbo, the famous Italian aviator, landed his fleet of 20 ships on his famous trans-Atlantic flight of planes across the Atlantic. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), a former minister of transport, started the first telephone cable across the Atlantic which was landed at Clarenville.
One of the first air strips in Newfoundland was built at Harbour Grace and was used considerably following the Lindbergh flight by fliers attempting to cross the Atlantic. It was from there that Old Glory flew to her doom and Amelia Earhart made her first crossing. This air strip could be used as an auxiliary airport.
At Bay de Verde is a large and important fishing settlement and the breakwater now under construction will be of great value to the fishermen. I am glad that steps are being taken to complete this breakwater so necessary for the fishermen in that area.
While from the point of view of general income of the people the fisheries are not as relatively important today as in the years past, the development of the pulp and paper industry, mines and the United States bases, as well as the acceleration of public works has created an economic value which has in sum total greatly outstripped the production value of the fisheries. On the other hand, no single industry or activity directly affects so many of the people as do the fisheries. In
430	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Tucker Newfoundland there are approximately 16,000 fishermen who live in more than 1,000 fishing communities along our 6,000 miles of coastline.
The major fishery activities are the frozen fish industry which depends entirely on the United States market for its distribution and the salt codfish industry which is almost entirely dependent on foreign currency markets; For centuries this was the only industry in Newfoundland and the people established their homes in small settlements along the coast where salting is the only feasible method for the preservation of the fish. Many of these places were built up, became quite important and achieved fair-sized populations because of that industry. Recently there has been a great decline in the value of that branch of trade which is adversely affecting a large number of our fishing population. The difficulties come from (a) the extreme competition of foreign salt fish producing countries which are taking a much larger share of the world's demand and (b) the difficulties of getting foreign exchange and import licenses in some of our principal markets.
In its foreign trade policy Canada should ldok at the urgent need of this industry and the numbers of people serviced by it in Newfoundland and conduct negotiations for exporting facilities to some of these countries as well as for the release of currency. Departments of government too often look at the sum totals of figures, that is, import and export values as between various countries, and not closely enough at the relative importance of certain industries in the support of large numbers of people who suffer badly if those industries are allowed to decline through lack of international trade facilities.
A particular problem now exists in that industry because of the complete closure of the Brazilian market because dollars are not available. The Department of Trade and Commerce should take a very close look at this problem and try to devise means whereby reciprocal trade can reopen that market for Newfoundland.
Third, there was a general trend away from Newfoundland fisheries by the people because of the difficulties of sale and the surpluses that often existed resulting in uneconomic prices. The application of unemployment insurance to fishermen started during the Liberal administration is having the effect of bringing a great many back to the industry, and it is particularly needed now because of the substantial lessening of the number of men in the woods operations of the pulp and paper companies. This makes it all the more necessary for a very active policy to be inaugurated in the marketing of

salt fish; otherwise there may be an unmarketable production which would set up a very great problem, not only for fishermen and the industry but for public administration as well.
Fourth, it is a general thought that the salt fish industry is outdated and does not merit aggressive promotional plans by the government and industry. This is all wrong. The world's consumption of salt fish has been increasing year by year and it is recognized as one of the major internationally traded products in the world. Some of the competing countries have been modernizing their production methods and building up their fishing fleets to the extent of operating floating factories and largely under the impetus of government planning and assistance. Very little of that has been in effect in the Newfoundland industry, notwithstanding the fact that the location for fishing is one of the best in the world.
The Department of Trade and Commerce has offices and permanent officials in most of the countries which consume Newfoundland products and it is very necessary for the economy of our province that these officials adopt a very aggressive policy in dealing with the government departments and the traders of these countries with respect to the handling of Newfoundland salted fish. It is a traditional trade and it is very important to note the slipping away which has been prevalent in past years. It is vital that this trend should be arrested and a strong promotional policy introduced. I am glad to relate, however, that since 1930 our fresh fish industry has greatly developed. In 1938 we exported about 500,000 pounds, while last year we exported more than 52 million pounds of fresh fish.
The federal governments have done much to assist our fishermen but much more assistance is required. When visiting my riding I have heard complaints about the lack of bait depots and docks. I understand the Department of Fisheries have in mind a^new bait program and I should imagine that consideration has already been given to the problem of bait supplies.
I would particularly like to have the erection of a bait depot considered in both South Port and Hants Harbour in Trinity bay. I should also like to see more wharves and breakwaters constructed in settlements where fishing is the main industry, not only in my riding but in all the ridings of Newfoundland and Labrador. Newfoundland fisheries rank among the richest and most important in the world and are undoubtedly one of our economic mainstays. We have in our fish industry a Klondike just as great as that of any gold claim in California or

even in the Yukon. It was Lord Bacon who said that the fisheries of Newfoundland are richer than the mines of Mexico and Peru.
Every year there are caught millions of dollars worth of codfish, herring, salmon, lobsters, squid, caplin, turbot, halibut, white-fish, seals and many other fish. With respect to our chief product, the codfish, we are losing some of our best markets owing to a lack of systematic way of marketing and curing the fish. For some years we have experienced competition in the fish markets of the world; every country is endeavouring to place their best products on the market. Only a few days ago Jamaica raised objection to our marketing and the codfish of Norway and Iceland are becoming of great importance, being subject to standard culls and superior curing and inspection.
There is no question that the codfish of Newfoundland is superior in every way but if our government does not institute a better way of curing and marketing of our fish and more uniform containers for our fish we will soon have to take second place. Our codfish is not up to the required standards set by our customers and no incentive has been offered our fishermen. They have not been encouraged or impressed with the importance of our fish being handled as a food product should be handled.
I regret to relate that we have much unemployment in Newfoundland. We have at the present time about 40,000 persons unemployed and approximately 18,000 drawing unemployment insurance. Less than half the unemployed still have unemployment insurance benefits and more people are unemployed without insurance today than the total number of unemployed a year ago. This condition is causing great hardship. Unemployment is a problem not easy to solve in my province; as indeed it is difficult to solve in any other part of our great dominion. We in the opposition hope a solution will soon be found, since unemployment affects all our constituents, indeed, all Canadians.
I would also like to mention the urgency of docking facilities for schooners and small craft. There are at least three communities where a slipway or dock could be built and used to good advantage by many fishermen and coastal traders in the riding of Trinity-Conception. Firstly at Catalina, which is fast becoming one of the most important fish centres of the island; secondly at Clarenville, which has a small shipyard and where a slipway could be very cheaply and easily constructed and would assist in producing employment and keeping the shipyard employees occupied which in turn would be of great benefit to the owners of fishing vessels and coastal schooners in the area; and thirdly
The Address-Mr. Morton at Harbour Grace, where there was at one time a slipway now out of operation.
In my opinion a slipway or floating dock should be placed at Harbour Grace as soon as possible to assist the fishermen who are returning to that occupation. In many of the above mentioned places there are skilled carpenters and shipbuilders who could provide valuable workmanship.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I bring you greetings from my riding and I would like to very sincerely thank the electors of Trinity-Conception for the honour they have conferred upon me and the confidence they have placed in me by electing me their representative in this House of Commons. I shall try at all times to be worthy of that honour and confidence by working for my riding in particular and my country in general.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first of all like to offer my congratulations to you upon your re-election to the post which you held with such great dignity and fairness in the last parliament. I also wish to congratulate the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Sevigny) and the Deputy Chairman (Mr. Rea) upon their election to posts of trust and responsibility and to commend the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) for their contributions to the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
At this time I would also like to pay tribute to the late John R. MacNicol who represented Davenport riding from 1930 until 1949. He served his riding well and many people still recall the many kindnesses and services which he rendered, not only to the people within his riding but throughout Canada.
I was somewhat sorry to hear that the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) was suffering from some hardships under the Conservative administration. I knew there were some hon. members on the other side of the house who would find difficulty in adjusting themselves to the fact that they are not indispensable and also to the realization that someone else can govern, not only as well as they but probably better. However, I can assure the hon. member that he and others need not be too much concerned, because I am sure this party will well look after those who are in the minority.
The riding I represent in the western part of Toronto has, like other ridings in the city of Toronto, become the home of many people of many racial origins who live side by side with our own Canadian people, and the melding of the many cultures which

The Address-Mr. Morton is taking place in this riding, as in other ridings across Canada, will produce the Canadian culture of the future. However, in this melding process we are faced with certain problems of integration of which I will speak at a later time.
Davenport riding, like other ridings, has its local problems. We share with other constituencies anxiety for those who are unemployed and who have difficulty in finding employment at this time. I should like in particular to bring to the attention of this house the difficulty experienced by one group of people who are finding it increasingly hard to readjust themselves and to obtain employment. I refer to those men and women who have entered upon middle age and who through no fault of their own have become displaced from their normal employment and cannot obtain new employment because of the working of what seems to be arbitrary pension schemes whose operations debar them from taking part in new fields of employment. I suggest that this situation is unfair to these people and results in a great waste of manpower in Canada. I realize that the solution to this problem does not fall within the jurisdiction of this house, but I would appeal to those insurance companies who sponsor such pension schemes to devise some form of transferable benefits so that these people may not be debarred from moving from one position to another. I urge, also, that the Canadian government should take the lead in adopting schemes which do not prevent people of middle age finding employment in new jobs.
Speaking of pensions, I should like to remind this house that in my riding many people are looking forward with great anticipation to the results of the present studies with regard to extending old age pension benefits.
In common with other areas, our riding has its housing problems. There are no vacant lots. Many of the people who formerly lived in the area have moved into the suburbs, while new Canadians and younger people have moved in. In an attempt to pay for their homes the newcomers have turned many single dwellings into multiple dwellings, which has caused overcrowding and even, in some instances, poor home conditions. It has also increased the problems which face our schools, and I would urge the government to conduct a more effective study of this question in co-operation with local authorities.
The new east-west subway on Bloor street will, when completed, pass through my riding. I know that representations are being made to the federal government for financial

assistance. This may, perhaps, be termed a local expenditure which does not qualify for federal assistance, but I must point out to the government that it is a manifestation of our national growth and deserves consideration. If direct aid cannot be given, the cost of this and other municipal projects should be borne in mind when increased grants are made to provincial governments.
I should like to turn to another subject about which I am greatly concerned, and to add my voice to those of many hon. members who have already spoken with regard to education. We can no longer escape the fact that education is a matter of national concern. We speak proudly of our great material resources, and we announce great plans for the development of those resources. We allot vast sums of money to open up our northland, we shout about the future of Canada, but we are silent on any bold scheme to develop the human resources which are so necessary in connection with all our great plans for the future.
We are spending billions of dollars annually in order to be prepared to defend our democracy from attack; we spent millions of dollars and thousands of lives in two world wars to protect this democracy, yet on the subject of education, which is a very necessary ingredient of our democracy, we seem to be afraid to risk our political lives and face the national problems of education which have to be solved. Many people avoid the problem on constitutional grounds.
As to the cost of education, I quote from the information bulletin put out by the Canadian Teachers' Federation research division in February, 1958, entitled "Educational Finance in Canada". Table 12 on page 21 estimated, after setting out the contributions of all levels of government toward all education in Canada, that in 1957 the total cost of education was $998.9 million of which the local school boards paid $416.8 million, provincial governments $437.1 million, the federal government $70 million and nongovernment institutions $65 million. The per capita cost of education is estimated to be $60, and the cost per member of the labour staff, $167. On page 28 of the same report the table shows the distribution of the net expenditures of all governments in 1955. Eleven point three per cent of those expenditures were devoted to education as compared with 38.6 per cent to defence and 14.3 per cent to social welfare. The table shows that expenditure on education is only a small proportion of the expenditures of all levels of governments; it is only one-third of the expenditure devoted to defence.

Mr. Speaker, I contend we have not done all we can within the framework of our constitution to meet this problem. In times of emergency the federal government has given assistance to education in the fields of agricultural, technical and vocational training. We have extended aid to our universities; we have provided scholarships on a dominion-provincial contributory basis and through the Canada Council. I agree that both federal and provincial governments must operate under the powers laid down by the terms of the British North America Act, yet I believe there is an over-riding responsibility upon the senior government to assess whether the component parts are meeting the changing needs of our country, otherwise, as a nation we will travel in parallel channels to oblivion. The time has come to re-assess whether the component parts of our government are meeting the needs of education.
While many members of the senior government bodies at the federal and provincial levels who are harassed by other problems appear on the surface to be quite complacent and self-satisfied that our educational problems, especially in respect to financing, are under control, many at the grass roots level are valiantly trying to stir up some action for financial assistance. A local politician was once asked by a frustrated trustee why it was that it was so much easier for a township to obtain money for roads than for education and he was told that when people ride over bumpy roads they get stirred up to protest and demand action. In education there are no bumps to stir them up. Perhaps the launching of the sputniks by Russia is the first real bump we have had in this field. It did at least stir up considerable interest in our shortcomings in the field of education.
But even before this prominent people were sounding warnings. I should like to quote Mr. James S. Duncan, a Canadian industrialist, who on December 10, 1956 presented the following conclusion of the exploratory committee of the industrial foundation on education in these words:
Canada is facing an educational crisis and because education is the foundation upon which our national strength and well-being are built, something must be done about it and done quickly. Fortunately the problem is not an insoluble one-in the simplest of terms-it is one of money, vast quantities of money; of buildings to house a rapidly expanding requirement for more schools, more teachers, colleges, more and larger universities, more technical colleges and particularly more qualified teachers. Of all these, the last is the most important.
I also wish to quote Joseph McCulley, warden of Hart House, University of Toronto, who when speaking at a directors' luncheon
The Address-Mr. Morton at the Canadian National Exhibition in August 1956, and as reported in the Globe and Mail of August 28 of that year, said:
Education should be a matter of national concern. The Ontario department of education has made herculean efforts to face the problem of crowded universities and other worries. But even all the efforts which have already been made are minimal compared with what must be done in the next ten years. If Canadian growth and development is not stopped in midstream we must face the fabulous cost of the education job that must be done. There is no justification for a Canadian educational system which deprives any child of the best possible education because of the accident of birth in one part of this country. The provincial governments and the federal government must face this problem.
To point out the need of financial assistance to students I refer to the findings of the teacher recruitment and service council for Ontario secondary schools as contained at page 6 of their brief presented to the industrial foundation on education in February 1957. As the result of a survey they found a large number of capable and ambitious students were unable to go to university because of lack of finances. Replies received from 236 schools in Ontario indicated there were 3,171 grade XIII pupils planning to attend university in 1957. In addition there were 2,146 grade XIII pupils with the capacity and ambition to attend university in 1957 but who were not planning to do so because of lack of funds. There were an additional 1,150 grade XIII pupils competent to attend university but who were not planning to do so,
The recent Canadian conference on education held in Ottawa in February of this year also discussed and pointed out the great needs of education. In its resolutions it indicated the need for the provision of funds for an adequate student aid program, the need for increased research and passed a resolution to the effect that representation be made to the appropriate authorities to the end that annual federal grants to universities be made on a more realistic and equitable basis to take into account the increasing proportion of student enrolment to the total population and the rising cost per student. They also urged that there be further aid forthcoming from the federal government either directly to the provinces or in some other way in order to assist them to finance the cost of education.
On the basis of the need and the importance of the above representation I strongly urge the government and this house to consider the necessity of exploring some means in co-operation with the provinces as to what further assistance may be given to education under the terms of our constitution without disturbing the local responsibilities for the administration of education and to provide equal

The Address-Mr. Nowlan opportunities for all those who have ability regardless of their financial position or geographical location.
Education in Canada today is like a jigsaw puzzle which needs to be placed together so that we can see a full and comprehensive picture of the problem. I urge the government of Canada to give leadership in bringing together all necessary parts to provide the comprehensive picture and provide Canadians the opportunities of fulfilling our appointment with destiny.
The people from coast to coast have caught the vision of the opportunities of building a greater nation. We cannot now waste time listening to those who brood in retrospect of what might have happened. We must now concentrate on what must happen if we are to fulfil our destiny and develop our God-given talents and resources in this country which provides unbounded opportunities for people who love freedom to work and live together as Canadians, united from coast to coast. I believe our party, under the leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker), can contribute much in the fulfilment of that destiny.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part for the first time in this debate I wish to tender the congratulations which have been uttered by so many hon. members and which continue to be so well deserved to the hon. members who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne, to Mr. Speaker, to yourself, as Deputy Speaker, and to those other officers who have been taking part in the proceedings of this house.
Within a few minutes this afternoon we will be having the first division of this session of parliament. In the case of over 100 hon. members it will be the first division in which they have participated and I am sure it will be an event of great significance to them, an occasion they will always remember. I believe it is fitting that they look upon the occasion of the first division in this way,
I know that many people coming into this house, those in the galleries and sometimes hon. members sitting on the floor may sometimes feel that this debate becomes somewhat monotonous. They hear hon. members discussing various and divers matters affecting everything from their own constituencies to events and subjects of international importance and they perhaps conclude that it does not serve any useful purpose. However, I am sure that those who are present this afternoon and those who will be participating in this first division will realize that this is one of the two great hilltops over which we pass 
during a parliamentary session, those hilltops being the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne and the budget debate.
The origin of the throne speech debate, of course, goes back to those historic times when rulers were apt to demand of parliament the things they desired by means of an address or a speech and sometimes over the years with great fear and trembling and at considerable risk the members of parliament finally evolved the mechanism of having an expression of thanks in the form of a speech, also including in that speech any matter they thought was worthy of comment, before the house settled down to deal with the matters which the sovereign had ordered them to take up. That is the historical background of the division which is coming up this afternoon, the first of the divisions which will occur in this debate, and although listening to speeches on the address in reply to the speech from the throne tends to become somewhat boring it is nevertheless a tradition we should revere and treasure because it is out of such traditions that many of our freedoms and particularly our parliamentary system have flown.
This debate will continue for some days. It is more than a matter of courtesy that a minister of the crown should arise on this occasion to answer the criticisms and deal with some of the suggestions which presumably have been made during the course of the debate.
I am frank to say, as you undoubtedly have noticed, that I have not been in this house as much as I would like to have been during the course of this debate because of the meetings of the various boards and committees on which one has to serve from time to time. But I have last night and this morning attempted to scan, rather hastily it is true, and to read over all of the speeches which have been made during this debate, particularly by those hon. members on the other side of the house. I must say that the diet which has been put before us has not been one which has been too robust. It savours a little bit of thin gruel and it has not been one to which one could make any considered reply.
Now, I can have some sympathy, of course, with the opposition. I, too, as well as some of us on this side of the house, have sat over there after going through one, two, three disastrous defeats and I know it is not the easiest thing in the world to come back and take too dogmatic a part in a debate of this nature immediately following an election such as we had on March 31. I do not think we would be too immodest, Mr. MAY 23, 1958
Speaker, if I did say that possibly we, although we were in that position, perhaps spoke with more pointed criticism and perhaps more forcefully than has been done on this occasion. That, of course, was not owing to the fact that we possessed any more ability than hon. gentlemen opposite but was simply owing to the fact that we had much more to criticize than they have had to criticize during this debate so far.
There is another factor, of course, which must add to one's appreciation of the position in which hon. gentlemen find themselves. So much has happened in the political sense that it is almost impossible to realize that it was less than a year ago when hon. gentlemen opposite were still sitting in the ivory towers of their embattlements here in Ottawa. The leaders were sitting here with a host of private troops complacently wondering whether the opposition might increase their strength to 50, 60 or 70, or perhaps might even lose and come back with fewer numbers than they had before. That was the attitude up until June 10 when the atomic bomb burst and on March 31 it was the hydrogen bomb.

We have heard it suggested that some of our friends who are here from Quebec are here because of the influence of the provincial government of Quebec. All I can say, is that if Mr. Duplessis is responsible in any degree at all for the election of the members from the province of Quebec, then he must be very, very proud of the calibre of men that he has sent here because certainly we are, and we appreciate very much to have them from that province.
I am not too bothered or too worried about such statements. I have been in this house for quite a while. I was president of the party for some time during those days when
The Address-Mr. Nowlan we did have disastrous defeats. I remember in 1949 we heard a great deal about the Drew-Duplessis axis. It somehow did not function. In 1953 we heard about the Drew-Duplessis axis. It did not function. Then, in 1957, our friends opposite who were then on this side of the house were discussing some iniquitous deal which was worked out between the leader of the opposition at that time and the premier of Ontario. It was going to represent something which was detrimental to Canada, and that did not function. The truth of the matter, of course, is that our friends opposite when they were in power did believe in the idea of dividing and ruling and did not maintain that degree of national unity which this country deserved. It was on that basis that they attempted to keep themselves in power for a substantially long while.
Now on this side of the house and on the other side we have the representative of the two great historic races which founded and built this country in the days gone by, and we also have the representatives of various races of new Canadians, all sitting here and taking their places as members of the House of Commons and representing their various constituencies.
It has been suggested from time to time- I have read it in the papers-that it is too bad that there is an overwhelming majority on one side of the house and a weak opposition on the other-I mean weak numerically. I must say if hon. members opposite are looking for data to that effect they can find quite a bit of it in the speeches of some of us in days gone by when we were speaking from that side of the house. Whatever may be the merits of the question as to a strong opposition or a weak opposition, I do think that as against that the fact that we have this tremendous group, representative of those races, coming here determined to serve this country and to work in the interest of national unity means that a greater contribution toward unity has arisen out of this than out of any other action which has been taken in the past or any other contribution really that this parliament can make to unity in the future. We are not the party of the Union Nationale, Mr. Speaker, but we are the party of national unity, and we intend to develop it and foster it.
We have also heard a great deal, of course, about unemployment. It has been talked of in various degrees by hon. members opposite but not in the doom and gloom accents that we heard during the election when we were told that there was a national disaster facing this country, when some hon. members opposite, and more who are not here-I remember
436	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Nowlan one former cabinet minister, the then member for Coast-Capilano, speaking all over the country and saying he was convinced that the number of unemployed at that time was in excess of a million and might easily reach a million and a half before March. All sorts of exaggerated and radical statements such as that were made. Now that the heat of the election is over I am sure that hon. gentlemen opposite, good Canadians as they are, appreciate the word which came out during the last two days showing a decided drop in unemployment figures in this country.
I am not minimizing it. Unemployment to the man who is unemployed and to his family can be a tragedy and there are many of those in this country today, more than we would like to see. It is true the tragic element of it has been mitigated to some extent in many instances by the extension of unemployment benefits, by the increased social welfare payments, and so on and so forth. But certainly the situation is improving rapidly and it is not one which approaches in any way the suggestion of a national disaster.
What were the figures we saw the other day? On April 18,-and these are the last official figures we have; undoubtedly the situation has improved a great deal since then which is a month or more ago-there were
516.000	men and women unemployed in this country; that is a lot of people. However, the labour force of this country had increased by 221,000 during the year, a substantial portion of which had arisen out of the immigration which took place last year. If the labour force this year were the same as last year, if it had not been for this tremendous increase, we should have had only 295,000 unemployed. I am not trying to argue syl-logistically. I realize that someone will say figures can be used in various ways.
These are the basic facts. There would have been 295,000 unemployed on the basis of last year's labour force. On the same date last year our friends in the Liberal government had 306,000 unemployed; that was on April 18. What did we hear about that? We heard that the country was in the throes of the greatest era of prosperity that had ever been known. We were told "You never had it so good."

speechtext:
That may be; I am quite sure that if the Liberals had remained in power long enough we would have had a maximum of unemployment and no population at all. There is no question about that.
Those are the figures. As I said, taking it at its worst, there were 516,000 unemployed on April 18. This figure has undoubtedly been substantially reduced by now. This is not the first time we have had unemployment in this country. I was interested in knowing what our friends said about these figures in 1954-55, figures which were roughly comparable to the figures today. I looked up Hansard and I found that the Right Hon. Mr. Howe spoke about this matter and, as recorded at page 2104 of Hansard for February 15, 1954, said:
As a result unemployment climbed to a level higher than had prevailed in any previous postwar year. Immediately the alarmists among us began to clamour for measures to offset a pending depression. The government did take action to extend unemployment insurance benefits, but no major anti-recessionary program was put into operation.
The Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, speaking earlier at page 1407 of Hansard for January 25, 1954, said:
Nothing is being done now except the increased endeavours of the various employment agencies throughout the country to find employment for those who have registered with them.
We have increased the unemployment insurance benefits, and we have done many other things to provide employment. Our friends opposite, some of those who are here this afternoon, cheered very loudly and pounded their desks most lustily when the Right Hon. Mr. Howe and the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent made those statements in the house. I wonder if their sympathy for the unemployed, different from what it was a few years ago, may be in part attributable to the fact that they too, at least in part, find themselves somewhat unemployed. There is, at least, a change in their attitude between the time when they sat over here and today, and that is perhaps something worth commenting upon.
They say, of course, that the government has done nothing. I am not going to deal with

the matter of housing. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) in piloting the bill through the house the other day referred to that at considerable length. He pointed out the many Steps that this government has taken and the substantial amount of money which we have made available, and are making available for housing. This, of course, is of direct assistance to the unemployed in this country. Perhaps one or two figures bear repetition. In the first four months of 1957, when our friends were in power, the housing starts totalled 12,800-plus. The housing starts for the first four months of this year were 25,300-plus. We are told that this government has done nothing, but it has more than doubled the record of the last government. These figures apply only to the towns and municipalities with a population of over 5,000. We have not got the figures, or at least the figures are not available for municipalities less than that.
However, that is not the entire story. As you well know, Mr. Speaker, provision has been made for the building of houses by the lower income groups. Provision has been made for lower down payments to encourage the building of houses and enable people in these income brackets to own their own homes. In addition to that it is expected that during the next few years this country will have an increase in population of 7 million to 8 million. It is necesary to carry on the tremendous housing projects, reorganization of our cities and removal of slum areas to take care of this increase. This government, under the aegis of the minister who has been in charge of this work, has initiated studies in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal and Halifax which will lead to slum clearance in those cities. I am very glad to say that in some of them, particularly in the city of Halifax in which I have a more than academic interest, there is work going on today in connection with a vast slum clearing project which will be of tremendous importance to the city and to that province in the future.
Now, they say our public works program is routine. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) said there was very little contained in the public works program which was not routine and a great deal of embellishment had been given this program by the government which was not justified. I noticed on the financial page of the Gazette this morning the financial editor, Mr. John Meyer, had this to say about the public works program of this government:
The list of make-work projects in the throne speech was impressive and has already given the country a confidence in an early recovery which was not apparent prior to the opening of parliament.
The Address-Mr. Nowlan
I think a statement like that, coming from the financial editor of one of the leading newspapers of this country, is at least of equivalent weight to that of the hon. member for Laurier in dealing with the value of the public works program of this country.
What is being done in public works? I am not going to enumerate all those things now. There is, of course, a need for public works to help unemployment. I am not suggesting for one moment, neither has the government ever suggested, we intend or could provide enough public works to provide employment for everyone in this country. Business and industry all have to play their part in this connection. What is needed is confidence, courage, leadership and the co-operation of all; then unemployment can be defeated. I have not any doubt that leadership is being given by this government and that courage is being restored to the people of this country.
They talk about depression and recession, all those words which they said one dare not use. I have here the figures for personal savings; the people are putting their money in the banks. I have figures for only the first two months of this year because those were the latest which one could get from the bureau of statistics. In January of last year savings deposits amounted to $6,039 million, while in January of this year they amounted to $6,322 million. In February of 1957, deposits had risen to $6,096 million. In February of this year it was $6,400 million, an increase of $78 million. Does that sound as if our economy was in the throes of a recession? Doth that sound as if times were so bad?
Take retail sales which are considered to be an index of business activity. In the month of January last year retail sales amounted to $1,030 million. In the month of January this year, with all the attendant troubles of which we are told and which we recognize, retail sales were $1,091 million, an increase of over $60 million. In February of last year retail sales were $999 million plus and in February of this year $1,016 million. In fact, retail sales today, so current newspaper reports say, are at the highest level ever known in Canada's history. The same is true of expenditures of various kinds.
We are told that the government had failed in the marketing of Canada's wheat. When this government came into power less than a year ago we inherited a carryover of 730 million bushels of wheat, the largest carryover in Canada's history. Our exports had declined by 47 million bushels to 262 million

The Address-Mr. Nowlan by the end of that crop year and this government certainly cannot be held responsible for that because that year ended in July, 1957. Despite the very aggressive sales campaign carried on by the United States and whether or not we agree that it will result in good for Canada as Mr. Benson tries to argue, we had sold substantially more wheat by January of this year than we had sold up to that time last year, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) is confident that by the end of the crop year on July 31 this year we will have sold over 300 million bushels of wheat. That is some achievement in view of the competition, increased cost and the prices with which we have to contend all over the world.
There is talk about a depression and the fact that car sales are down. Yesterday afternoon I happened to have in my office an executive officer of one of the big three car manufacturers in Canada. He told me that his company had sold more cars in April of this year and was selling more now than it had ever sold before in their history in this country. As far as the other companies are concerned, sales generally have picked up despite the fact that in the United States, so we are told, car sales are 35 per cent below what they were last year.
As I have said, car loadings are up, automobile sales are up, personal savings are up, retail sales are up. Every yardstick ordinarily used by economists indicates continuing expansion and development in this country.
In that connection I think it is interesting to look at a report in the Montreal Gazette of a statement made by Mr. Robert Green. I am not sure whether or not he is a relative of the Minister of Public Works but I doubt it because he does not live in this country. He is one of the vice-presidents of the Prudential Insurance Company of America, a company with some financial experience and knowledge, I would think. This is what Mr. Green had to say about the relative economic positions of Canada and the United States, and you would almost think it was the Minister of Public Works speaking. It is not a direct quotation but a report of his remarks which appeared on the financial page of the Montreal Gazette yesterday. It reads:
Robert M. Green, vice-president in charge of Canadian operations for Prudential Insurance Company of America, believes that Canada has turned the economic corner and is on its way out of the recession. He says this conviction is formed from the results of the surveys conducted by Prudential's economists in both Canada and the United States. Of greater significance, however, is Mr. Green's belief that Canada will lead, not follow, the United States towards recovery,
IMr, Nowlan.j
I think a statement such as that made by a man of his eminence, experience and position should go a long way to answering the criticisms we have heard in the house during the last few days of this debate. We are told that there should be tax reductions. Economists differ on that matter but I am going to point out that we have had tax reductions. During the session last fall we reduced taxes by $187 million which is no small amount and so what we are being urged to do we have already done. During the election campaign I did not hear any of the speeches of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) but I read some of them and I was somewhat intrigued by his advocacy of a reduction in taxation of $400 million as something which would achieve wonders. Yet we have been told in the House of Commons that a reduction of $187 million in taxes was nothing at all. However, $187 million is almost half of $400 million and my mathematics indicate that twice nothing is still nothing. Therefore if our reduction was nothing the $400 million was certainly nothing when it was advocated on the election platform. In any event, we have reduced taxes.
There is talk about aid to municipalities. How many scores of millions of dollars were made available by this government to the provinces and then turned over to municipalities? I know in my own little province of Nova Scotia over $3 million of the $10 million the province got was made directly available to the municipalities, and I am sure the same thing applies to all the other provinces.
One could go on and develop this matter further but I think I have said enough to indicate that this government has been giving leadership to Canada in the difficult days through which we are passing, leadership which I believe is appreciated and recognized by the Canadian people. I believe that with the faith and courage the Canadian people have always shown and working together this country will go on to carry out highway programs, northern development and all the other matters which are envisaged. With the establishment of national unity, with a plan for the future, with leadership such as the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) is giving to the country, there is every reason to look forward with confidence to Canada's development and we will continue to grow and expand during the years ahead in a way in which our forefathers and even we ourselves have never envisaged in the past.

They do seem to constantly express the feeling that the government is letter perfect and that nothing ever happened before June 10, 1957, but that feeling is not quite in accord with the facts.
I want to deal with some of the things which did happen since June, 1957, and which were the responsibility of the previous government headed by the present Prime Minister. I have spoken of the matter of unemployment and have mentioned that except for the minister who immediately preceded me no minister of the crown has spoken about the subject in this debate although there was one rather interesting interjection yesterday when my colleague, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), was speaking. His remarks appear at page 360 of Hansard of May 22, when he said "There is unemployment which is far above the normal seasonal unemployment level". This was a simple statement of fact but the interjection of a minister of the crown, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Browne), was "So what?"
Then what was the solution offered by the minister who spoke today? He referred to a document put out jointly by the Department of Labour and the bureau of statistics dealing with most recent unemployment statistics. I think this document was dated May 21 and he referred to its contents as "good word". Is it good word when we are given official figures indicating, according to the bureau of statistics, that those without jobs and seeking work number 516,000 or, according to the figure used by the unemployment insurance commission, that those registered as seeking employment totalled 825,000 as of April 19 last? Is that good word? It is not good word at all; it is a very serious matter. He went on at some length to try to prove that if there had not been an increase in the labour force these unemployment figures would not have been so high. That was so illogical that I am sure after reflection-

No, it is not logical at all. It was a simple error into which he fell in trying to prove that if there had not been any population there would not be any unemployment. I am sure that is not what he intended. I think I can appreciate the point he was trying to make, but that is not what he intended to say, I am sure.
The causes of unemployment are varied and I realize that some of these causes are of a nature that they arise outside of Canada and are not under the control of the government. I grant that at once, but there are some causes of unemployment which do lie within the control of the government and some of those causes should be examined and we should seek to do what we can to remove them. That is the responsibility of the government and I, for my part, would like to discuss what I apprehend to be some of those causes.
I would now like to refer to a subject I mentioned earlier, one of the two hilltops, a rather picturesque phrase chosen by my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue; that is to say, the budget.
What is the history of this new government? What is its record since history began on June 10, 1957? Let me tell the hon. member who interrupted me a few moments ago that the history is that the party of which he is a member, led by the present Prime Minister during the whole of the last parliament of Canada did not see fit to bring forward a budget. Let me seek to show him that this fact contributed materially to the unemployment which exists today, and let me try to indicate in what way I believe that to be true.
There is another aspect of this matter. I take the view, of course, that the Prime Minister was departing from constitutional practice by his failure to have a budget delivered during the last parliament, particularly when he was not defeated in that parliament and was not forced to call an election. But that is not the point I am stressing at the moment; that is a constitutional issue.

No, I have a good memory on the point, and I am quite prepared to debate it with the hon. member any time he wishes.
The traditional budget performs three main functions in our system of government. It provides a statement of accounts for the fiscal year; it provides a financial forecast for the coming year, giving certain economic data; and, in addition to those two things, it sets forth the whole fiscal, financial and taxation policy of the government. That is its traditional function.

We have heard a great deal in recent months about the Conservative party having assumed the responsibility of office on June 21, 1957, for the first time in 22 years. I should have thought-and I believe many people in the country shared this opinion- that a situation of this kind would lead to changes in fiscal and financial policy. I should have thought that one of the first things the new government would have sought to do would have been to bring forward its changes in fiscal and financial policy and to expose to parliament and the public what those changes were, together with their implications to business and industrial life. Indeed, that is what business in this country did expect. And when the budget was withheld and did not come forward business firms one by one took decisions not to proceed with various projects whose development they had in mind. They took decisions to delay work on those projects for the time being, and those delays meant that men who might have been at work on those projects today were never put to work on them.
I regret very much that decision by the Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), not to present a budget-and I know that before the Prime Minister is through this parliament he will have occasion, on his own responsibility as Prime Minister, to regret it. I admit, of course, that the refusal to expose these matters to parliament or to the country may have been successful in helping the Conservative party in its re-election, in that no opportunity was provided for criticism of its financing. That may be true and seeing the vast array of hon. members opposite and to my left I admit that it was certainly successful. But it was a high price to pay for success if it added to the numbers of the unemployed, as it undoubtedly did.

subtopic: "DO IT NOW" EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM
"DO IT NOW" EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
How much money, if any, was spent from October 1, 1957, to date, in promoting winter
employment through the so-called "Do it now. why wait for spring" program?
Answer by: Hon. Michael Starr (Minister of
Labour):
$166,576 in paid advertising was purchased by the Department of Labour including the unemployment insurance commission since October 1, 1957, for the promotion of winter employment through the program for combating seasonal employment.
I would like to point out that this expenditure represents only a small proportion of the total cost of the publicity campaign which was developed with the support of the provinces, municipalities, industry, labour and a great number of organizations at both national and community levels. The manner in which the newspapers, magazines, radio and television stations, motion picture theatres and outdoor advertising companies offered public service support to the "Do It Now" campaign last winter is deserving of the highest commendation. At the same time, business operators, particularly those connected with building and construction, took advantage of the general promotion campaign to increase their advertising to promote the idea of taking advantage of the availability of men and materials during the winter lull. The result was that the advertising and publicity program conducted by the government was increased more than tenfold throughout Canada.

Monday, May 26, 1958
